## Why the best teams win

The model trained on 256 knockout team-seasons to predict progression using group and league-phase data from 488 total seasons. Its predictive capability shows a mean within-season Spearman correlation of 0.46 between predicted and actual stages, with an AUC of 0.72 for reaching the final. The model correctly identified finalists in its top four predictions 46.7% of the time across the 15 analysed seasons. Its Brier score is 0.098, which compares to a base-rate guess Brier score of 0.103, indicating a marginally better fit without claiming statistical superiority.

Regarding what drives deep runs, the "style" feature set yields the highest Spearman correlation at 0.41 among single categories, while the "results" set achieves an AUC of 0.72. The most important stat by average SHAP contribution is Attacks per game with a value of 0.25, followed by Goal difference per game at 0.201 and Long passes (% of passes) at 0.137. All three are marked as robust, meaning the logistic model agrees on their direction in at least 12 of 15 seasons. Passes per game also ranks highly with an importance of 0.128 and a robust label. Conversely, stats like Fouls committed per game (lower is better) have lower importance at 0.088 but are marked model-dependent rather than robust. The data suggests that high-volume attacking metrics and positive goal differentials are the strongest statistical associations with reaching later knockout stages.

## Winners vs runners-up

When comparing group and league-phase stats between winners and runners-up across all 15 finals, no single difference reaches significance under the Holm-adjusted p threshold of 0.05. The largest mean z-score difference appears in Fouls committed per game (lower is better), where winners were lower in 12 of 13 non-tied cases with a value of -1.13, yet the adjusted p-value remains at 0.181. Similarly, Pre-season UEFA club coefficient shows a mean difference of 0.57 with winners higher in 13 finals, but the p-value is 0.111. Other metrics like Shots per game show winners were higher in 11 cases with a z-score of 0.79, while Passes per game and Pass accuracy both show winners higher in 12 cases with z-scores of 0.97 and 0.76 respectively; all these comparisons yield p-values well above the significance threshold.

The comparison reveals that even stats where winners consistently outperformed runners-up do not achieve statistical significance after adjustment. For instance, Points per game shows a mean difference of -0.01 with an equal split of 7 wins and 7 losses, resulting in a p-value of 1.0. Goal difference per game has a z-score of 0.22 with winners higher in 9 cases, also yielding a p-value of 1.0. Even the stat where winners were lower more often, such as Long passes (% of passes) at -0.42, fails to reach significance. The data indicates that while there are observable trends in specific metrics like fouls or pre-season coefficients, none of these differences between finalists can be confirmed as statistically significant based on the provided Holm-adjusted p-values.

messages.content: You are a football performance analyst writing for a curious, data-literate reader. Use ONLY the facts provided. Quote every number exactly as it appears in the facts, with the same rounding. Do not introduce players, managers, matches, events, analyses or numbers that are not in the facts. 'Teams beaten (%)' figures say how many teams the club did better than on a stat, so higher is always better, including for stats marked '(lower is better)', where doing better means having the lower value. Write them as 'better than X% of teams', never as 'top X%'. SHAP contributions are measured in knockout stages: a positive contribution means the stat pushed the model's expected stage up by that fraction of a round, a negative one pushed it down. A SHAP contribution is the model's view, not a measure of how good the team was at the stat: a team can rank high on a stat the model marked down, so never call a stat a strength or a weakness because of its SHAP sign. Everything here is a statistical association, not a cause: never say a stat or a team's profile drove, powered, propelled, carried, helped, hindered or prevented a result, and do not explain why a stat got its contribution. Write plain markdown without tables.

Write 350-450 words of markdown in total, two paragraphs of about 100 words under each of exactly these two headings, in this order:
## Why the best teams win
## Winners vs runners-up

Explain which stats are associated with deep knockout runs and whether pedigree, results or style matters most, using the feature-set comparison. Say how well the model does by comparing its Brier score with the base-rate Brier score and stating how often finalists were in its top 4; the model's edge over the base-rate guess was not tested, so do not call it significant or superior. 'Importance' is the average size of a stat's push on the expected stage, in either direction. The model learns from the knockout team-seasons, using each team's group/league-phase stats. Only call a stat 'robust' if its robustness label is robust. Winners vs runners-up compares those same group/league-phase stats, not what happened in the final. Never call a winners-vs-runners-up difference significant unless its Holm-adjusted p is below the significance threshold in the facts.
